Age-period-cohort-improvement (APCI) model

Source: R/model-apci.R
apci.Rd

The stochastic implementation of the APCI model of Richards, Currie, Kleinow and Ritchie (2019), fitted per stratum: log m[x, y] = alpha[x] + beta[x] (y - ybar) + kappa[y] + gamma[y - x] (eq. 8), with ybar the mean of the years of the data. The model needs at least five single years of age, without an open interval, and at least ten years (package-specific, for the choice of the ARIMA models).

Usage

apci(smooth = TRUE, kappa_order = NULL, gamma_order = NULL)

Arguments

smooth

Smooth alpha and beta over age with P-splines, the smoothing parameters chosen by BIC (Richards et al. 2019, Table 1).

kappa_order, gamma_order

ARIMA orders c(p, d, q) of the models of kappa and gamma (without a mean). NULL (default) chooses them as in Richards et al. (2019, Appendix E).

Value

A model specification.

Details

Following the paper:

  • the deaths are Poisson with mean m[x, y] times the central exposure (eq. 4), and the parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood (Section 3);

  • cohorts with four or fewer observations get gamma = 0 and are not estimated (Appendix B);

  • five identifiability constraints (Appendix C): sum(kappa) = 0 (eq. 17), sum((y - ymin) kappa) = 0 (eq. 21), and sum(w gamma) = 0, sum(w (c - cmin + 1) gamma) = 0 and sum(w (c - cmin + 1)^2 gamma) = 0 (eq. 19, 20 and 22), with w the number of cells of cohort c. With the corner cohorts fixed at 0, only the constraints on kappa are needed; the constraints on gamma restrict the fit (the paper's over-constrained model, Section 6). The estimates maximise the likelihood subject to all five constraints, which hold exactly. For the paper's 55 ages and 45 years, the unsmoothed model then has its effective dimension of 241 (Table 2);

  • with smooth = TRUE (the paper's APCI(S), Table 1), alpha and beta are P-splines over age (Eilers and Marx 1996) with penalties on the second-order differences of their coefficients (Appendix D; Appendix G calls the penalties quadratic), and the two smoothing parameters minimise the BIC, deviance plus log(n) times the effective dimension, with n the number of cells (eq. 24). kappa and gamma are not smoothed. With smooth = FALSE, every age has its own alpha and beta;

  • kappa and gamma are projected by ARIMA models without a mean, fitted with stats::arima() to the estimates as if they were observed (Section 5, Appendix E). By default the orders are chosen as in Appendix E: for kappa, the ARMA orders p, q in 0 to 3 with the smallest AICc for d = 1 and for d = 2, then of these two the model with the smaller root mean squared error (Solo 1984); for gamma, the orders p, q in 0 to 3 with the smallest AICc for d = 1. gamma is projected for the cohorts born after the last estimated one, which include the youngest cohorts with four or fewer observations (Appendix B). The two processes are independent;

  • draws are simulated paths of both ARIMA processes, with their coefficients at the estimates. The paper adds parameter risk by a bootstrap of the mean of the process for kappa only, and the APCI processes have no mean (Appendix E). alpha, beta and the estimated kappa and gamma are fixed, so the deterministic part beta[x] (y - ybar) continues linearly. Predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates.

Package-specific (reference unknown): the B-splines are cubic with equally spaced knots about five years of age apart, on the range of the ages widened by 1% at each end (as p_splines(); the paper does not give the knots); the smoothing parameters are searched between 1e-4 and 1e10 with the search of p_splines(); the estimates come from penalised iteratively reweighted least squares with the constraints as Lagrange conditions (the paper: the algorithm of Currie 2013, with the constraints as rows of an augmented model matrix); the AICc counts the ARMA coefficients and the innovation variance as parameters, on the differenced series, as forecast::Arima(); the root mean squared error that chooses d is taken over the one-step residuals from the third year, which both orders of differencing have; ARIMA paths are simulated from the state-space form of the fitted model, from the filtered state at the last estimate. The paper's value-at-risk framework and annuity factors are not implemented.

References

Richards SJ, Currie ID, Kleinow T, Ritchie GP (2019). A stochastic implementation of the APCI model for mortality projections. British Actuarial Journal 24: e13. doi:10.1017/S1357321718000260

Eilers PHC, Marx BD (1996). Flexible smoothing with B-splines and penalties. Statistical Science 11(2): 89-121. doi:10.1214/ss/1038425655

Currie ID (2013). Smoothing constrained generalized linear models with an application to the Lee-Carter model. Statistical Modelling 13(1): 69-93. doi:10.1177/1471082X12471373

Solo V (1984). The order of differencing in ARIMA models. Journal of the American Statistical Association 79(388): 916-921. doi:10.1080/01621459.1984.10477111

See also

stmomo() for the age-period-cohort and Renshaw-Haberman models.

Examples

# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("StMoMo", quietly = TRUE)) {
  ew <- mt_subset(as_mt_data(StMoMo::EWMaleData), ages = c(55, 90), periods = c(1971, 2011))
  fit <- mt_fit(apci(), ew)
  p <- mt_parameters(fit)
  p[parameter %in% c("order_kappa", "order_gamma")]
  fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 10, n_draws = 200, seed = 1)
  life_expectancy(fc, at = 65)
}
